sentences.text: The genus Deltadromeus contains only one known species, D. agilis, which is known from an incomplete postcranial skeleton.
This fossil record lacks most vertebrae, ribs, and forelimbs, leaving much of the animal's anatomy unknown.
A recent 2025 study noted that the specimen lacks a femoral crest, a feature commonly seen in ornithomimids like Struthiomimus and Gallimimus.
Based on the holotype, the animal was approximately 8 meters long and weighed 1050 kilograms.
In 2001, Frank Seebacher estimated the holotype to be 8 meters long and weigh approximately 1050 kilograms.
The tibia-to-femur length-to-diameter ratio in Deltadromeus is 0.95, compared to 0.76 in Allosaurus and 1.16 in Ornithomimus.
The genus Deltadromeus was described by Sereno and colleagues in 1996.
American paleontologist Paul Sereno and colleagues described the genus Deltadromeus in 1996.
The species D. agilis was described by Sereno in 1996.
Fossils definitively assigned to Deltadromeus were discovered in 1996 by Paul Sereno during an expedition in the Kem Kem Beds of eastern Morocco.
The holotype specimen, cataloged as SGM-Din 2, was an incomplete postcranial skeleton found at a single site.
Deltadromeus fossils were discovered in 1995 by Gabrielle Lyon during an expedition led by Paul Sereno in the Tegana Formation of Morocco.
Deltadromeus was a carnivore with unusually thin hind legs for its size, suggesting it was a fast runner.
If Deltadromeus is closely related to herbivorous or omnivorous ceratosaurs like Limusaurus, it may have been herbivorous or omnivorous.
Isotopic evidence suggests carcharodontosaurids and ceratosaurs in the Kem Kem Beds and Elrhaz Formation consumed sizable terrestrial animals.
Researchers suggest niche partitioning occurred among theropods, with spinosaurids eating fish and other groups hunting herbivorous dinosaurs.
Abelisauroid affinities suggest Deltadromeus may have been omnivorous or herbivorous.
If omnivorous or herbivorous, Deltadromeus and Bahariasaurus may have filled a niche typically occupied by ornithischians.
The diet of Deltadromeus cannot be confirmed because no skull material has been found.
Originally classified as a basal coelurosaur related to Ornitholestes, this classification has been challenged by later studies.
Many studies since its description have considered Deltadromeus to be a ceratosaur, though researchers disagree on the specific type of ceratosaur it represents.
A 2016 analysis suggested Deltadromeus and Gualicho were sister taxa within the family Neovenatoridae.
Some subsequent studies classified Deltadromeus as a ceratosaur, though they did not include Gualicho in their analysis.
Deltadromeus is tentatively classified in the suborder Ceratosauria.
Sereno and others described Deltadromeus as a basal coelurosaurian in 1996, but Rauhut placed it within ornithomimosaurians.
The Paleobi Database lists the parent group of Deltadromeus as Noasauridae.
Fossils of Deltadromeus date to the Cenomanian stage of the Cretaceous period, approximately 100 to 95 million years ago.
Deltadromeus lived during the Cenomanian stage, from 100.5 to 93.9 million years ago.
During the Cretaceous, North Africa was covered in mangrove forests and wetlands, supporting diverse fish, crocodyliforms, and pterosaurs.
Deltadromeus fossils are found in the Kem Kem Beds of North Africa.
Deltadromeus fossils are also found in the Bahariya Formation of Egypt and the Elrhaz and Echkar Formations of Niger.
During the mid-Cretaceous, North Africa was a mangrove-dominated coastal environment with vast tidal flats and waterways bordering the Tethys Sea.
It is debated whether Deltadromeus and Bahariasaurus are distinct genera or if one is a synonym of the other.
Some studies suggest Deltadromeus may be a junior synonym of Bahariasaurus, though this is not universally accepted.
It is debated whether Deltadromeus is a distinct genus or merely a synonym of the poorly understood dinosaur Bahariasaurus.
